title: Walnut cheese board
subtitle: A serving board with a turned-edge juice groove
excerpt: A cheese and serving board in seasoned walnut: 35 cm by 22 cm, 20 mm thick, with a 5 mm juice groove routed around the perimeter and a routed hanging hole. Walnut is the prestige serving-board species: dark, fine-grained, and spectacular at table. Plane and scraper finish, danish-oil treatment.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
A thin steel plate with a turned burr edge used to take very fine shavings from a wood surface, leaving a cleaner finish than sandpaper.

content.text: A walnut cheese board is a serving platter with enough presence to anchor a table. At 35 cm by 22 cm, it holds a full cheese selection without crowding, and the juice groove catches moisture from cut cheeses and sliced fruit. This project uses
walnut: the choice is aesthetic as much as functional. Walnut's near-black grain with pale sapwood streaks is distinctive in a way that no other British commercial timber matches.

Walnut PAR board, 22 mm thick (planed to 20 mm). Cut a 37 cm by 24 cm blank, leaving 2 cm on each dimension for waste during flattening and edge finishing. Walnut from a single board gives the most consistent colour; book-matched walnut (two boards opened like a book from the same section) is more complex but requires edge-jointing. For a first walnut board, a single board section is the simplest approach.

Plane the top face with the No. 4 smoothing plane. Walnut planes very cleanly with a sharp iron; the grain is usually straight enough that direction does not matter. Traverse the first pass diagonally and the second at 90 degrees to the first. Use the
for the final pass: walnut's open grain benefits from scraping rather than abrasive paper, which embeds grit in the pores.

Square the four edges with the block plane. The board should be 35 cm by 22 cm when the edges are trued. Check with a combination square. Chamfer all long-grain and end-grain edges with the block plane: 3 mm chamfer on the top edges, 2 mm on the underside.

The juice groove runs 2 cm from the board edge, all the way around the perimeter. It is 5 mm wide and 4 mm deep. The groove can be routed with a trim router and a straight bit, or cut by hand with two parallel cuts from a marking knife and a chisel to remove the waste between them. Mark the groove lines with a marking gauge before cutting, and cut the end-grain sides (across the grain) with a sharp chisel to define the shoulders cleanly.

Use the corner of the card scraper or a narrow chisel to clean the inside of the groove. The groove bottom should be smooth and flat, not rough from chisel tearout. A smooth groove drains to the corners rather than holding pools.

Apply danish oil to all surfaces including the groove interior and the underside. Three coats over three days. Cure for five to seven days before food contact. Walnut absorbs the first coat quickly; on the face of a walnut board, the difference in appearance after three coats versus one coat is significant: the grain fills and the depth of colour increases markedly.

attrs.symptom: The juice groove corners have tearout at the end-grain sides
attrs.cause: The chisel was not sharp enough for the cross-grain cuts at the corners.
attrs.fix: Hone the chisel before cutting the groove shoulders at the end-grain sides. Score the shoulder line with a marking knife first to sever the fibres.

attrs.symptom: The board is slightly cupped after oiling
attrs.cause: The oil was applied to one face only first, raising the moisture content on one side before the other.
attrs.fix: Always apply oil to both faces at the same time. If cupping has started, oil the concave face and stack the board flat under weight while the oil cures.
